messages.subject: inla.mesh.2d() very slow
parts:
Hi all, 

I'm finding the inla.mesh.2d to be running at a glacial pace on anew project I"m working on, and I'm not sure why. This is my code:

mesh = inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain=loc.mesh, max.edge=c(0.3,0.6), offset=c(1,1))

There are 20,245 coords in the loc.mesh matrix. I left it to run on a Linux server overnight and it didn't finish. 

Many thanks,
Julianne

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.mesh.2d() very slow
parts:
Hi,
Possible causes depend on the details of the input data. What’s the extent of loc.mesh? E.g. summary(loc.mesh) ?
For some input geometries there may be special cases that lead to infinite loops, which I think is the likely reason in your case, since 20000 isn’t very large, and if Max.edge implies a very large output, it would be likely to run into memory issues instead of just keep working. See the help text for information on an option that can limit the maximum mesh size; that doesn’t prevent infinite loops, but does guard against accidentally large meshes.
The special geometries that cause infinite loops can usually be avoided by defining the mesh boundary with inla.nonconvex.hull instead of the plain “offset” method.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: inla.mesh.2d() very slow
parts:
Per my experience, I will say check the units of your coords e.g whether it is in meters, km etc.  inla.mesh.2d runs at a slower pace when i run decimal values (like yours) and coords in meters. So I use this approach 

mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bdry, max.edge=c(5000,15000), cutoff=3000)

I remember reading somewhere the values in the inla.mesh function must correspond to your coords units (I stand corrected)
